tldr: We introduce FCTS, a framework that feeds the local terrain geometry and robot state from quadruped traversal failures back to an LLM to automatically generate terrains targeting specific weaknesses, while using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore optimal curriculum branches. On challenging rubble terrain modeled after real-world sites, FCTS drastically boosts traversal success rates over baselines and transfers successfully to a physical robot.
hero_caption: An overview of the FCTS system. Traversal failure data on a fixed validation terrain (robot pose, local elevation maps, camera images, etc.) is extracted, and a multimodal LLM generates terrain code targeting those weaknesses. MCTS then explores promising policy checkpoint trajectories in parallel during reinforcement learning.
overview:
Quadruped parkour has made remarkable progress, but training curricula are usually limited to canonical obstacles like stairs and hurdles. As a result, when faced with irregular environments like disaster and construction sites filled with compound bumps, fissures, and slopes, policies fail abruptly due to limited generalization.

To tackle this, the authors focus on diagnostic failure data: "where and why did the robot fail?" Instead of aggregated average scores, the 3D geometry and robot pose at the failure site are passed to a multimodal LLM to automatically generate new training terrains that address these weaknesses. In addition, Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is applied to curriculum discovery to efficiently determine which checkpoint should advance to which terrain under a fixed training budget.

Evaluated on challenging benchmark courses 3D-scanned from real construction and disaster sites, FCTS dramatically raises success rates from 28.4% to 85.8% on a medium-difficulty course, and from 14.9% to 44.7% on a hard course compared to top baselines. Furthermore, it successfully traverses a composite parkour course on a physical Boston Dynamics Spot robot, showing excellent sim-to-real transfer.
contributions: Proposed a failure-conditioned curriculum generation mechanism that generates training terrains based on the robot's failure coordinates, termination mode, pose, and local elevation map.
Formulated an MCTS framework where policy checkpoints are nodes and terrain generation plus RL execution are edges, incorporating rehearsal of past successful terrains.
Achieved traversal performance that significantly outperforms existing parkour and LLM curriculum baselines on unseen, challenging benchmarks built from scanned real-world data.
Demonstrated zero-shot transfer of policies learned in simulation to a composite parkour setup on a physical Boston Dynamics Spot robot.

sections.heading: How can we overcome irregular real-world terrain that canonical training cannot handle?
sections.summary: Traditional quadruped learning relies on human-designed canonical obstacles, causing trained policies to easily fail in complex real-world composite terrains. To resolve this bottleneck, FCTS uses an LLM to automatically generate terrains tailored to policy weaknesses from specific failure contexts, using MCTS to search the learning path.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning for quadruped parkour has achieved amazing agility, such as leaping over gaps and vaulting high obstacles. However, these were only learned within carefully tuned, predefined terrain families. In real construction sites and disaster zones, irregular bumps, narrow footholds, and steep inclines appear simultaneously. In other words, the biggest constraint was not the robot's physical ability, but what terrain distributions it saw during training.

Redesigning these by hand takes tremendous effort. Recently, methods like Eurekaverse have emerged to automatically generate terrain code using Large Language Models (LLMs). But prior methods only fed aggregated numerical values like average traversal scores back to the LLM. As a result, the LLM could not know where or why the robot fell, often producing arbitrary terrains based purely on its own priors.

This work returns to the core insight that the moment of failure is the most valuable diagnostic signal. By feeding the LLM the failure coordinates, the robot's pose at the time of failure, and the surrounding local elevation map, the system synthesizes terrains that pinpoint weaknesses. Given that running RL training is computationally expensive, the authors developed FCTS, a framework that uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to efficiently explore branching checkpoints.

captions.F1: Traversal comparison on an unseen rubble course reconstructed from real-world scans. Baseline methods (Extreme Parkour and Eurekaverse) fall or stop early near waypoints 3–4, while the policy trained with FCTS (green) clears all waypoints to complete the course.

sections.heading: At the intersection of parkour learning, environment design, and LLM generation
sections.summary: This section reviews three research areas: quadruped parkour, Unsupervised Environment Design (UED), and LLM-based code generation. FCTS integrates these within a novel framework featuring localized failure feedback and MCTS in the policy checkpoint space.
sections.details:
This research builds upon three main lines of prior work.

### Quadruped Parkour Learning
Works like Robot Parkour Learning, ANYmal Parkour, and Extreme Parkour (EP) have demonstrated remarkable agility, acquiring diverse skills like jumping and climbing. However, these methods adjust difficulty schedulers inside predefined obstacle parameter spaces, unable to invent new terrain structures altogether.

### Automated Curricula and Unsupervised Environment Design (UED)
Frameworks such as GoalGAN, PAIRED, and POET automatically generate environments matched to an agent's current capabilities. In terrain locomotion, methods like TACL learn difficulty functions over existing maps, but stay confined to predetermined parameter spaces or procedural generation rules.

### LLM-Based Curriculum Generation and Search
Eureka, Eurekaverse, and EnvGen leverage the expressive power and reasoning of LLMs to generate RL environments and reward code. Other works like GIF-MCTS use MCTS to search code generation. However, most previous code tree searches evaluated lightweight code execution. In FCTS, a single branch expansion (edge) represents a full RL training run, creating a fundamental distinction: it searches the improvement trajectory of policy checkpoints rather than a pure code space.

sections.heading: Creating terrain from failure and growing policies with tree search: The FCTS algorithm
sections.summary: FCTS operates outside existing parkour learners and runs MCTS guided by a fixed validation environment. Based on geometric and pose data gathered during failure diagnosis, an LLM generates three terrain types—targeted, generalized, and composite—while rehearsing past successful terrains to develop the policy.
sections.details:
Here is an overview of FCTS and the key steps of its algorithm.

### III-A Preliminaries and Validation Terrain Design
Given a base policy $\pi_0$, an RL trainer $\mathcal{T}$ runs on generated terrain curricula $\mathcal{C}_i$ to yield new checkpoints. Because each training run is computationally heavy, the best policy must be found within a fixed training budget $N_{\mathrm{train}}$. To fairly compare policies with different training histories, a fixed validation terrain set covering standard parkour challenges (box climbs, gap jumps, narrow pathways, etc.) is prepared in advance with an LLM and used as an invariant yardstick.

### III-B Failure-Guided Curriculum Tree Search Steps
In the search tree, each node $s_i$ represents a policy checkpoint, and edges represent RL training runs.

- **Selection**: To balance unexplored and promising branches, the PUCT rule selects the parent node for the next expansion.
- **Failure diagnosis**: The selected policy runs in parallel ($R=512$ rollouts) on the validation terrains. To avoid being misled by outliers, the system identifies the mode failure distance, recording coordinates, termination cause, nominal robot pose, an $8\,\mathrm{m} \times 8\,\mathrm{m}$ local elevation map, and camera images.
- **Expansion**: To prevent catastrophic forgetting of past capabilities, terrains that previously drove performance gains are pooled, and 50% of the training terrains are allocated to rehearsal. For the remaining 50%, the LLM receives the failure context and branch history to output three terrain programs: (1) a targeted terrain reproducing the failure, (2) a generalized terrain varying it, and (3) a composite terrain combining both.
- **Simulation & Backpropagation**: Since a child node's true value lies in how much further it can improve, shallow parallel rollouts of depth $H=2$ estimate future performance. A Max-backup strategy, evaluating the highest performance in the branch, updates the parent value.
- **Parallel search**: Because training is slow, adding in-flight counts to visit counts enables asynchronous parallel exploration, increasing throughput.

captions.F3: Evaluation routes in the two reconstructed environments. On the left, in the Debris site, routes from Easy to V-Hard are automatically designed based on terrain relief statistics. On the right, in the Exposed Beam site, evaluation routes are set manually because large openings and narrow beams are ill-suited for continuous relief calculation.

sections.heading: Overwhelming traversal on collapsed buildings and beams, plus transfer to physical Spot
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted on unseen scanned environments mimicking industrial and disaster sites. FCTS achieved an 11.4% completion rate and high progress on the hardest debris course where baselines fell below 1%, while also proving the efficiency of parallel MCTS and successful transfer to a real Boston Dynamics Spot robot.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Two environments scanned from real construction and disaster sites were used: the Debris site and the Exposed Beam site. These are completely unseen environments never used during training or terrain generation. Baselines include Extreme Parkour (EP) as a representative human-designed curriculum, Eurekaverse with evolutionary LLM generation, and Modified Eurekaverse equipped with validation environment information.

### IV-A Traversal Performance in Reconstructed Environments
On the relief-categorized routes of the Debris site, FCTS demonstrated commanding performance:
- **Easy**: $84.0\%$ completion rate (strongest baseline: $31.5\%$)
- **Hard**: $44.7\%$ completion rate, interquartile mean (IQM) progress of $0.82$ (strongest baseline: $14.9\%$, IQM $0.42$)
- **V-Hard**: While baselines stalled below $1\%$ success, FCTS achieved an $11.4\%$ completion rate and reached an IQM progress of $0.71$ (baselines topped out at $0.44$).

### IV-B Why Does FCTS Clear Obstacles Where Baselines Fail?
Qualitative analysis showed the performance gap stems not from average walking across the course, but from specific compound bottlenecks. Examples include a 90-degree turn over mixed debris and holes, a slope with rounded boulders, and broken hurdles with consecutive drops and gaps. Tracing the best FCTS search branch shows that geometric elements needed to overcome failures—such as undulating debris, then sloped pillars, then elevated blocks and voids—were introduced into the curriculum incrementally and compounded.

### IV-C Parallel Search Efficiency & IV-D Real-Robot Transfer
Under a fixed 24-hour compute budget, parallel MCTS increased expansion throughput by roughly 5.3x compared to sequential search (from 0.21 to 1.13 expansions per hour). Additionally, a physical Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with an Intel RealSense D435i and Jetson AGX Orin traversed a composite course of pallet climbs, block steps, and stair descents smoothly and stably using the zero-shot simulation policy at 50 Hz.

captions.F4: Three bottlenecks where baselines fell (90-degree turn, sloped debris, consecutive gaps) and the curriculum evolution along the best FCTS branch. Incorporating failure feedback produced terrains with staged difficulty—undulations to sloped pillars to elevated blocks—enabling the robot to master composite terrains.
captions.F5: Hardware experiments using a physical Boston Dynamics Spot. A single policy trained with FCTS smoothly traverses a composite parkour course—climbing pallets to an elevated block, then descending stairs—with 50 Hz onboard control.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: By combining LLM terrain generation conditioned on localized failure diagnostics with MCTS, FCTS dramatically improves quadruped traversal on unseen, severe real-world terrains. The method offers a powerful framework for automatically building curricula tailored to robot weaknesses.
sections.details:
This paper presented FCTS, a new automatic curriculum generation method for quadruped parkour. Moving beyond terrain generation driven by broad scores, it provides the LLM with rich diagnostic data—specifically the robot's pose and local geometry at the point of failure—enabling the synthesis of training terrains that target specific weaknesses.

Furthermore, considering the heavy compute cost of RL, it introduces MCTS to explore promising checkpoints while rehearsing past successful terrains. This demonstrated traversal performance far surpassing prior methods on scanned environments modeled after real disaster and construction sites, and transferred successfully to a physical Spot robot.

As a future direction, the authors plan to move beyond controlled indoor experiments to field trials deploying robots directly in actual industrial and disaster sites.

takeaways: In LLM environment generation, providing localized failure signals like local elevation and robot pose at fall locations is far more effective than broad average scores.
Exploring checkpoints as a tree with MCTS, rather than through greedy unidirectional updates, prevents local optima and training dead-ends.
Allocating around 50% of training terrains to rehearsal of past successful terrains is critical to preventing catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired skills.

Success on difficult terrain hinges on a handful of compound bottlenecks rather than average gait, so accumulating targeted fixes yields dramatic jumps in overall completion (e.g., from under 1% to 11.4%).
limitations: Because each tree expansion requires a full RL training run, computational requirements remain very heavy even with parallelization.
On extremely discontinuous environments (such as Route 1 in the Exposed Beam site), FCTS lagged behind the baseline Eurekaverse in completion rate, showing performance can vary by terrain type.
Hardware validation was performed on a controlled indoor composite course with pallets and stairs; testing in real disaster or industrial sites with mud and collapse hazards remains future work.
